issues.legal_issue: A guardian’s contract to purchase property on behalf of a minor for the minor’s benefit is enforceable despite the minor’s incapacity to contract and the asserted lack of mutuality.
material_facts: The minors’ mother and guardian entered into an agreement on their behalf to purchase a house, and part of the price was paid as earnest money.
The seller failed to perform, and the minors sued for specific performance and deposited the balance of the price after the trial court decreed the suit.
The High Court dismissed the suit on the ground that a contract made on behalf of minors lacked mutuality.
The benefit of the transaction to the minors was not disputed before the Court.
issues.conclusion: The guardian’s contract on behalf of the minors was enforceable, and the trial court’s decree for specific performance was restored.
issues.legal_principle: A minor cannot contract personally, but under Hindu law a natural guardian may contract on a minor’s behalf for necessity or the minor’s benefit. Section 8 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 permits a guardian to do acts necessary, reasonable and proper for the benefit of the minor or the minor’s estate; that power is not narrower than the power recognised under Hindu law. Section 11 of the Contract Act does not exclude such guardian-made contracts, and the English rule based on want of mutuality does not apply. The Court relied on Krishnaswami v. Sundarappayya and Srikakulam Subrahmanyam v. Kurra Subba Rao, among other authorities, and explained the earlier decision in Mir Sarwarjan v. Fakhruddin Mohd. Chowdhary in light of the later authority.

predicates.specific_performance_claim: A claimant seeks specific performance of an agreement made on behalf of a minor.
predicates.guardian_contract_for_minor: A guardian entered into the agreement on behalf of the minor.
predicates.contract_benefits_minor: The agreement is necessary, reasonable and proper for the benefit of the minor or the minor’s estate.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance claim concerns a guardian’s agreement made for a minor and the agreement benefits the minor, the agreement is enforceable.

issues.legal_issue: A guardian’s agreement to purchase property for a minor does not impose a prohibited personal covenant on the guardian merely because the purchase price must be paid.
material_facts: The guardian agreed on behalf of the minors to purchase property and the agreement required payment of the balance of the price.
The seller argued that the payment obligation was a personal covenant prohibited by Section 8 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, relying on Section 55(5)(b) of the Transfer of Property Act.
The Court found that the guardian had entered into the agreement within the guardian’s competence and on behalf of the minors.
issues.conclusion: The payment obligation was the minor’s liability under the Transfer of Property Act, not the guardian’s personal covenant, and that objection did not prevent enforcement of the contract.
issues.legal_principle: Section 8 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 does not make a guardian’s competent contract on behalf of a minor a personal covenant of the guardian merely because payment is required. Under Section 55(5)(b) of the Transfer of Property Act, the liability to pay the purchase price in this transaction was the minor’s liability; the agreement was entered into effectively on the minor’s behalf.
